passages.¶1: Framing: from a conversation with Omid; author is not a security expert; an end-user attempt to understand.
passages.¶10: Proton residual risk: malicious client code (web app or update) could capture the typed password before hashing; with the stored encrypted key, that decrypts everything. Trust requires matching open-source code, no compelled future injection, uncompromised infrastructure.
passages.¶11: Crucial difference: Proton lacks directly usable keys and must compromise the client first; WhatsApp's server can directly grant key access to any device it authenticates.
passages.¶12: Signal options: (1) Android manual local backup, an encrypted file guarded by a 30-digit passphrase, physically transferred; (2) direct device-to-device transfer with both present; (3) newer Secure Backups encrypted with a 64-character recovery key Signal never sees.
passages.¶13: Signal servers can never grant history access; even cloud backups open only to the on-device recovery key. Genuinely zero-knowledge: no decryption, no recovery help if the key is lost.
passages.¶14: Password layer: even trusted encryption leaves the plaintext-password question; with password plus encrypted key, everything decrypts.
passages.¶15: Client behavior is checkable if open source, but server-side fate after arrival is not: code closed, audits only cover the audited deployment, rogue employees and breaches remain possible.
passages.¶16: Precedents: Facebook logged hundreds of millions of passwords in plaintext for years (2019); Adobe's 2013 breach exposed plaintext hints; smaller services use plaintext or unsalted MD5.
passages.¶17: Proton reset evidence: email/SMS password reset destroys old-email access, suggesting genuine inability without the password; still not proof, possibly image-preserving refusal.
passages.¶18: Core lesson: trust rests on reputation, jurisdiction, business model, behavior, not verifiable guarantees. Attack surface shrinks WhatsApp to Proton to Signal recovery keys (device or key compromise only).
passages.¶19: Comparison table. Keys generated on-device for all three. Private keys: WhatsApp encrypted on servers with server-grantable keys (server-mediated escrow); Proton encrypted on servers by user password (password-encrypted storage); Signal on-device or under unseen recovery key (client-controlled). New device: WhatsApp server grants keys; Proton ships encrypted key for local decryption; Signal needs physical transfer or unseen 64-char key. Rogue device: YES for WhatsApp, NO for Proton (short of malicious client) and Signal. Trust and models as in ¶18.
passages.¶2: E2EE definition: encrypted on sender device, decrypted on receiver device, never decrypted in transit. Against men-in-the-middle most implementations suffice; but users usually want no outsider, especially the provider, reading content. WhatsApp metadata (network, frequency, volume, timing) still aids interpretation.
passages.¶20: Password section, short answer: we don't know for certain whether companies avoid plaintext storage.
passages.¶21: Verifiable: open-source clients (hashing before sending, though silent on servers); Wireshark traffic inspection (plaintext over the wire is a flag, HTTPS hides server fate); audits (trusted auditor, trusted deployment).
passages.¶22: Unverifiable: closed server code (even shown code may not be running); later updates can add logging; rogue employees or breaches can inject it.
passages.¶23: Signals: good (open-source servers, published audits, clean breaches); bad (password reset preserving old data, security through obscurity, past privacy violations).
passages.¶24: Cases: Adobe 2013 (plaintext hints aided brute force); Facebook 2019 (200-600 million plaintext passwords searchable by 20,000+ employees, some archives from 2012; claimed unintentional, no abuse found); small services (plaintext or unsalted MD5, discovered at breach).
passages.¶25: Trust becomes unnecessary only if: all crypto is client-side (Signal-style recovery keys); the server sees nothing decryptable (zero-knowledge proofs); code is open, reproducibly built, and verifiably running.
passages.¶26: Applied: WhatsApp demands trusting Meta's infrastructure, password handling, government-response, and breach security; Proton demands proper hashing, no pre-hash logging, uncompromised infra, plus honest clients; Signal demands little beyond secure implementation and keeping the recovery key.
passages.¶27: Bottom line: prefer client-side encryption, open-source everything, decentralized minimal-trust systems, and hardware keys like YubiKey that never expose secrets.
passages.¶28: Sources: Meta multi-device engineering (July 2021); Proton key-storage and zero-access docs; Signal Secure Backups blog (September 2024) and support page.
passages.¶3: WhatsApp answer: unclear. If implementation matches claims with no secret backdoors, Meta cannot read content; but closed source blocks negative certainty. Given its business, the 2021 policy sharing data for ads across Meta, and the 2019 plaintext-password failure, near-certain access is the reasonable read.
passages.¶4: Smoking gun: can history move across devices without manual key transfer? Encryption means a public locker plus a receiver-only master key; a second device should not magically hold it. Signal forces key copying; any Facebook touch of the key equals a door-key copy on a public billboard.
passages.¶5: WhatsApp: server stores encrypted history plus account-to-device mappings; new devices are authenticated by the server and handed decryption keys. Safeguards (device lists, security codes) rely on honest server reporting, which could hide a rogue device.
passages.¶6: Proton: private key is generated in the browser, then encrypted with the user password using bcrypt and AES-256 before server storage. The encrypted private key lives on Proton servers, not only the original device.
passages.¶7: Proton login in six steps: type password; browser bcrypt-hashes it with server-provided salt; hash goes to Proton for authentication; server returns the encrypted private key; browser decrypts it locally with the original password; mail becomes readable.
passages.¶8: Hashing (authentication) is one-way and irreversible; encryption (private-key protection) is two-way and reversible with the key. The key wraps in the actual password, not its hash.
passages.¶9: Theory: Proton sees only the hash for login, which should not decrypt the password-wrapped key.

meta.title: Let's Talk Privacy: who can read your messages

nodes.text: Encrypted chats still trust providers; only client-held keys minimize that trust.
E2EE means device-to-device secrecy, but users need provider exclusion, not just transit safety.
Non-expert end-user inquiry from a conversation with Omid.
Metadata (network, frequency, volume, timing) still aids interpretation.
If claims hold with no backdoors, Meta cannot read; closed source blocks certainty.
Business model, 2021 ad-sharing policy, and 2019 plaintext failure imply near-certain access.
Smoking gun: history on a new device with no manual key transfer.
Locker plus receiver-only master key; server key touch equals public billboard copy.
WhatsApp server stores encrypted history and hands keys to devices it authenticates.
Device lists and codes rely on honest reporting; a rogue device could hide.
Proton generates the private key in-browser, wrapping it with bcrypt and AES-256.
Six-step login: type, bcrypt with server salt, authenticate, fetch key, decrypt locally, read.
Hashing authenticates one-way; encryption protects two-way under the actual password.
In theory the seen hash cannot decrypt the password-wrapped key.
Malicious client code could capture the typed password before hashing.
Trust needs matching code, no compelled injection, uncompromised infrastructure.
Proton must steal the password first; WhatsApp grants keys directly.
Signal: 30-digit passphrase file, device-to-device transfer, or unseen 64-character key.
Android backup needs physical transfer; direct transfer needs both devices present.
Zero-knowledge: no decryption, no recovery help after a lost key.
Plaintext password storage cannot be ruled out with certainty.
Open clients prove sending behavior, never the server's later handling.
Facebook logged hundreds of millions plaintext for years; Adobe leaked hints; MD5 persists.
Proton reset destroys old mail, suggesting genuine inability, but proves nothing.
Trust rests on reputation, jurisdiction, model, behavior, not verifiable guarantees.
Escrow (WhatsApp) versus password-wrapped (Proton) versus client-controlled (Signal).
Rogue device: YES for WhatsApp; NO for Proton and Signal (client caveat).
Checkable: open clients, Wireshark traffic, audits of deployed code.
Uncheckable: running code, later updates, rogue staff, breaches.
Good: open servers, audits, clean breaches; bad: reset-proof data, obscurity, violations.
Facebook 2019: 200-600 million passwords, 20,000+ searchers, archives from 2012.
Trust ends only with client-side crypto, zero-knowledge servers, verifiable builds.
WhatsApp needs whole-infrastructure trust; Proton hashing honesty; Signal key custody.
Prefer client-side encryption, open source, decentralization, hardware keys like YubiKey.
Sources: Meta 2021 engineering, Proton key docs, Signal September 2024 backups.
